findings.title: The guard closed the throw, but opened one narrow predicate/move disagreement: a non-array order yields canMoveGroup=false while moveGroup returns []
findings.description: Round 1 finding 1 is fixed and the fix is sound — this is the one behavioural seam the fix introduced, and I own it: my round 1 recommendation asserted that with the guard in place "moveGroup already returns the order unchanged, so the existing agreement invariant is preserved for free". That claim was wrong on exactly this path. When `order` is not an array there is no order to return unchanged, so `const next = Array.isArray(order) ? [...order] : []` hands back `[]`, while `canMoveGroup` correctly reports `false`. The agreement property the round 2 commit set out to pin — predicate true exactly when the move changes the order — therefore does not hold here: can=false, yet the returned value differs from the input. Measured across the hostile-shape sweep, all 16 non-array shapes behave this way (null, undefined, {}, 'focus', 'focusBar', 42, true, function, array-like {0,1,length}, Set, Map, null-prototype object, Uint8Array, arguments object). Note the counterpart is clean: a non-array `hiddenGroups` with a valid `order` agrees perfectly (can=false, order returned unchanged) in all 16 shapes, because `next` is still a real copy. Two secondary points. First, the JSDoc on moveGroup now overstates the contract — "Если движение невозможно — возвращается копия исходного порядка" is untrue for garbage input, where an empty array is returned instead. Second, `[]` is a different normalization than the one the sanitization layer picked for the same situation: sanitizeGroupOrder(non-array) returns the full six-id default order (verified by direct call), not an empty array. Reachability is why this is minor and not major: sanitizeGroupOrder runs unconditionally on every load (src/data/migration.ts:153), so board.groupOrder is always a real array by the time any UI touches it, and Task 08 has no caller yet (grep for moveGroup/canMoveGroup finds only the definitions). Damage is also bounded even in the impossible case — I verified sanitizeGroupOrder([]) rebuilds the complete default order, so an empty array persisted into data.json is fully repaired on the next load.
findings.location: src/ui/groupOrderUtils.ts:68 (const next = Array.isArray(order) ? [...order] : []) and the JSDoc at :58-61
findings.impact: A future caller in Task 08 that writes moveGroup's result back without first consulting canMoveGroup would, on a non-array groupOrder, silently blank the board's group order for the rest of the session instead of leaving it alone. No persistence-level data loss (the next load's sanitizer restores the full default order) and no confidentiality or integrity consequence — this is an in-session rendering failure on locally corrupted data, on a path the sanitizer already makes unreachable.

findings.title: Duplicate ids in order break the same agreement invariant — arrow reports enabled but the move is a no-op
findings.description: Found while fuzzing the new code for the agreement property; not introduced by this commit, and not reachable today. When `order` contains the same id twice, `order.indexOf(groupId)` resolves to the first occurrence while the scan can select the second one as the swap target. The swap then exchanges two identical values, so `moveGroup` returns an array equal to its input while `canMoveGroup` returns true. Concrete case: order ['focus','focus','backlog'], hidden [], moving 'focus' down — canMoveGroup=true, moveGroup returns ['focus','focus','backlog'] unchanged. The exhaustive sweep over exotic-but-real arrays found 12 such disagreements out of 720 cases, every one of them from the duplicate fixture; no other real-array shape disagreed (subclassed arrays, sparse arrays with holes, frozen and sealed arrays, Proxy-wrapped arrays, empty and single-element arrays all agree, across every id and both directions plus a junk direction value). This is the exact user-visible symptom the visible-row-skips-hidden rule was written to avoid — a button that looks live and does nothing. Reachability is nil in the shipped path and that is why it stays minor: sanitizeGroupOrder deduplicates via a `seen` Set (src/data/migration.ts:21-28), drops ids outside GROUP_IDS, and backfills any missing id, so `order` reaching this module is always a clean six-element permutation. I verified this by direct call — sanitizeGroupOrder(['focus','focus','backlog']) returns the full deduplicated six-id order. Worth recording because the round 2 commit added a test titled "the predicate is true exactly when the move changes the order", and the property as stated in that title is not universally true; its nine fixtures are all duplicate-free, so the test passes without covering this case.
findings.location: src/ui/groupOrderUtils.ts:27 (order.indexOf resolves the first occurrence) vs :42-43 (the scan may land on a later duplicate)
findings.impact: On a hand-edited data.json that survived sanitization — which it cannot today — a reorder arrow would render enabled and do nothing when pressed. No data loss, no security consequence. The practical value here is documentary: the module's headline invariant depends on an upstream uniqueness guarantee that lives in a different task's file, and nothing in this module states that dependency.
findings.recommendation: No code change required while sanitizeGroupOrder owns uniqueness. Make the dependency explicit instead, so a future change to the sanitizer cannot quietly invalidate this module's contract — one line in the findSwap doc comment, e.g. "Инвариант «предикат ⇔ перестановка» опирается на уникальность id в `order`, которую гарантирует sanitizeGroupOrder." If you would rather not depend on an upstream guarantee at all, make the agreement structural by comparing positions instead of values: `if (order[i] !== groupId && !hiddenGroups.includes(order[i])) return { from, to: i };` — but note that is a behaviour change on inputs that cannot occur, so the comment is the better-proportioned fix.

findings.title: Carried over from round 1: hiddenGroups is still never sanitized — routing to Task 03 confirmed
findings.description: Re-verified and unchanged. At the audited commit d60e30c, the only code touching hiddenGroups anywhere in src/data/migration.ts is the version < 4 branch at :101-102, which replaces the value only when it is strictly `undefined` and does not run at all for data already at version 4 or above. The unconditional sanitization block at the end of migrateData still handles groupOrder and group titles only. I also checked the in-flight Task 03 working tree during this audit: it is being actively edited (surrogate-pair handling in sanitizeGroupTitle, a freshDefaultData helper), and hiddenGroups sanitization has not been added there yet either — so the finding is genuinely still open, not silently resolved elsewhere. I confirm the round 1 routing to Task 03 and I do not think this must be handled inside Task 04, for three reasons. First, ownership: the fix is a sanitizer function applied in migrateData's unconditional block, which is entirely Task 03's file and Task 03's established pattern — implementing it from Task 04 would mean editing another task's module for a defect that predates this one. Second, Task 04's own exposure is now closed on its side: after the round 2 guard, a non-array hiddenGroups can no longer make this module throw or silently switch `.includes` to substring matching, so groupOrderUtils is correct in isolation regardless of what the sanitizer does. Third, and decisively, the residual failure is not in Task 04's code at all — with `"hiddenGroups": null` in a v8 data.json, BoardSettingsPopup.svelte:14 throws on `[...board.hiddenGroups]` before groupOrderUtils is ever reached, so a guard added here would not fix the user-visible symptom. The sanitization layer is the only place that repairs it for every consumer at once. Task 04 should be closable without waiting on this.
findings.location: src/data/migration.ts:101-102 and :152-157 (asymmetry with sanitizeGroupOrder); consumed at src/ui/groupOrderUtils.ts:25,35,43
findings.impact: Unchanged from round 1: board settings become unreachable on a hand-corrupted or externally-synced data.json, with no message and no self-repair — the same class of failure Decision 6 was written to eliminate for groupOrder. Local availability only; no confidentiality or integrity impact. Task 04 is no longer a participant in this failure after the round 2 guard.

verificationEvidence.auditedCommit: d60e30c (verified in an isolated git worktree — see workingTreeNote)
verificationEvidence.noThrow: 0 throws across the full probe set: 16 hostile shapes applied to both `order` and `hiddenGroups` in both directions (null, undefined, {}, 'focus', 'focusBar', 42, true, function, array-like, Set, Map, null-prototype object, Proxy-of-array, Uint8Array, arguments object, Symbol.isConcatSpreadable object), 12 exotic-but-real array shapes crossed with 6 hidden sets, 7 group ids including undefined/null/'__proto__'/'constructor', and 5 direction values including junk; plus 7744 exhaustive fuzz cases over every order of length 0-4 from a 3-symbol alphabet crossed with all 8 hidden subsets, all ids and both directions.
verificationEvidence.predicateMoveAgreement: Holds for every input reachable through the sanitized path. Two exceptions found and reported as findings 1 and 2: non-array `order` (can=false, returns []) and duplicate ids in `order` (can=true, returns an equal array). Zero disagreements across all other real-array shapes — 720 targeted cases over subclassed, sparse, frozen, sealed, Proxy-wrapped, empty and single-element arrays.
verificationEvidence.noMutation: 0 input mutations across the entire probe set, checked by snapshotting every own property (not just JSON) of both `order` and `hiddenGroups` before and after each call. The returned array is never the same object as the input. Frozen and sealed input arrays are handled without throwing, which confirms writes land only on the local copy.
verificationEvidence.guardDidNotOpenAnything: Array-like objects ({0,1,length} with borrowed indexOf/includes), Set, Map, typed arrays, arguments objects and null-prototype objects are all correctly rejected by Array.isArray and take the fail-closed path. Proxy-wrapped arrays pass Array.isArray by design and behave identically to the underlying array. Subclassed arrays are accepted and normalized: the spread produces a plain Array (verified: output constructor is Array, prototype is Array.prototype), so no subclass behaviour survives into the result. Sparse arrays are accepted; holes read as undefined, are treated as visible entries and can be swapped with — harmless, and unreachable since JSON.parse cannot produce holes. No coercion hooks are invoked on elements: a poisoned object with valueOf, toString and Symbol.toPrimitive placed inside both `order` and `hiddenGroups` triggered none of them, confirming indexOf and includes use strict/SameValueZero comparison and open no user-code execution path. The one hook that is reachable is Symbol.iterator via the `[...order]` spread, which a crafted Array subclass can override — not reachable from JSON.parse, which yields only plain arrays, and the result is overwritten by the swap assignments regardless.
verificationEvidence.prototypePollution: Round 1 conclusion holds. Canaries on Object.prototype and Array.prototype were unchanged after driving arrays containing '__proto__', 'constructor' and 'prototype' as both element values and as the moved groupId, and after passing a JSON.parse'd {"__proto__":{...}} object as `order`. The two write sites are next[swap.from] and next[swap.to], where both indices come from indexOf or a bounds-checked loop counter and are therefore always integers within [0, length), so no string key can ever be assigned. A '__proto__' element travels through as an ordinary string value: moveGroup(['__proto__','focus'],'focus','up',[]) returns a plain array ['focus','__proto__'] with Array.prototype intact.
verificationEvidence.termination: Round 1 conclusion holds. The single loop moves by a fixed step of -1 or +1 with bounds checked on both sides, over an array that is never mutated during iteration, so it is monotone and bounded by order.length. A junk direction value falls through to +1 rather than 0, so it cannot stall. A 50000-element all-hidden worst case completed in 3ms. Repeated application converges: 100 successive moves over the six real ids reached only 4 distinct states before repeating.
verificationEvidence.regressionClosed: The round 1 substring symptom is confirmed fixed. canMoveGroup(['backlog','focus'], 'focus', 'up', 'focusBar') now returns false (fail-closed) where the pre-fix code would have let 'focusBar'.includes('focus') report the group hidden and drive the arrow from the wrong rule.
verificationEvidence.testSuite: 22/22 pass at d60e30c, run in an isolated worktree against tests/unit/groupOrderUtils.test.ts only. tsc --noEmit is clean.
